claim: Angiomotin (Amot) was originally identified as an angiostatin-binding protein involved in the regulation of endothelial cell polarization, migration, proliferation, and angiogenesis.
source: Angiomotin (Amot) was originally identified as an angiostatin-binding protein involved in the regulation of endothelial cell polarization, migration, proliferation, and angiogenesis (Kikuno et al., 1999; Levchenko et al., 2003; Troyanovsky et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Kikuno et al., 1999; Levchenko et al., 2003; Troyanovsky et al., 2001).

claim: Amot is expressed as two isoforms generated by alternative splicing, full-length Amot-p130 and truncated Amot-p80, which lacks the 409-amino acid N-terminus.
source: Amot is expressed as two isoforms generated by alternative splicing, full-length Amot-p130 (referred to as Amot in this manuscript) and truncated Amot-p80, which lacks the 409-amino acid N-terminus (Ernkvist et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ernkvist et al., 2006.

claim: Amot, Angiomotin-like 1 (AmotL1) and Angiomotin-like 2 (AmotL2) compose the Motin family of proteins.
source: Amot, Angiomotin-like 1 (AmotL1) and Angiomotin-like 2 (AmotL2) compose the Motin family of proteins, which share an N-terminus with conserved glutamine-rich domains and PPxY motifs, and a C-terminus containing conserved coiled-coil (CC) and PDZ-binding domains (Bratt et al., 2002; Nishimura et al., 2002; Zheng et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Bratt et al., 2002; Nishimura et al., 2002; Zheng et al., 2009).

claim: The Motin family proteins share an N-terminus with conserved glutamine-rich domains and PPxY motifs, and a C-terminus containing conserved coiled-coil (CC) and PDZ-binding domains.
source: Amot, Angiomotin-like 1 (AmotL1) and Angiomotin-like 2 (AmotL2) compose the Motin family of proteins, which share an N-terminus with conserved glutamine-rich domains and PPxY motifs, and a C-terminus containing conserved coiled-coil (CC) and PDZ-binding domains (Bratt et al., 2002; Nishimura et al., 2002; Zheng et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Bratt et al., 2002; Nishimura et al., 2002; Zheng et al., 2009).

claim: The functions of Motin family members appear to be distinctive, as divergent spatiotemporal and expression levels have been described across human and mouse tissues and cell lines for each of the family members.
source: Although structurally similar, the functions of Motin family members appear to be distinctive, as divergent spatiotemporal and expression levels have been described across human and mouse tissues and cell lines for each of the family members (Moleirinho et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moleirinho et al., 2014.

claim: Amot is required for endothelial cell migration, by binding to the Syx:Patj/Mupp1 polarity complex to localize RhoA activity to the leading edge of migratory cells.
source: Functionally, Amot is required for endothelial cell migration, by binding to the Syx:Patj/Mupp1 polarity complex to localize RhoA activity to the leading edge of migratory cells (Ernkvist et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ernkvist et al., 2009.

claim: Amot has been implicated in epithelial cell polarity, as an inhibitor of the GTPase-Activating Protein (GAP) Rich1.
source: It has also been implicated in epithelial cell polarity, as an inhibitor of the GTPase-Activating Protein (GAP) Rich1 and shown to compromise the integrity of tight junctions by promoting Rich1-mediated hydrolysis of Rho GTPases Rac1 and Cdc42 (Wells et al., 2006; Yi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wells et al., 2006 and Yi et al., 2011.

claim: Amot compromises the integrity of tight junctions by promoting Rich1-mediated hydrolysis of Rho GTPases Rac1 and Cdc42.
source: It has also been implicated in epithelial cell polarity, as an inhibitor of the GTPase-Activating Protein (GAP) Rich1 and shown to compromise the integrity of tight junctions by promoting Rich1-mediated hydrolysis of Rho GTPases Rac1 and Cdc42 (Wells et al., 2006; Yi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wells et al., 2006 and Yi et al., 2011.

claim: Amot regulates collective migration of epithelial cells as part of a signaling axis composed of Merlin-Amot-Rich1 and the Rac1 small GTPase.
source: Amot regulates collective migration of epithelial cells as part of a signaling axis composed of Merlin-Amot-Rich1 and the Rac1 small GTPase (Das et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Das et al., 2015.

claim: At tight junctions, TJ-associated Merlin inhibits Rac1 activation through the Amot-Rich1 axis.
source: At tight junctions (TJ), TJ-associated Merlin inhibits Rac1 activation through the Amot-Rich1 axis, relocalizing Merlin to the cytoplasm during cell migration and releasing Rac1 from a suppressed state (Das et al., 2015; Yi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Das et al., 2015 and Yi et al., 2011.

claim: Merlin relocalizes to the cytoplasm during cell migration and releases Rac1 from a suppressed state.
source: At tight junctions (TJ), TJ-associated Merlin inhibits Rac1 activation through the Amot-Rich1 axis, relocalizing Merlin to the cytoplasm during cell migration and releasing Rac1 from a suppressed state (Das et al., 2015; Yi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Das et al., 2015 and Yi et al., 2011.

claim: Amot directly binds to YAP via 106LPTY109/239PPxY242 motifs present in the N-terminal domain of Amot-p130 and WW domain present in YAP.
source: Amot also directly binds to YAP, a central effector of the Hippo signaling pathway, via 106LPTY109/239PPxY242 motifs present in the N-terminal domain of Amot-p130 and WW domain present in YAP (Yi et al., 2013, 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yi et al., 2013, 2011 and Zhao et al., 2011.

claim: The Hippo-YAP signaling pathway, originally characterized in Drosophila, is highly conserved in mammals.
source: The Hippo-YAP signaling pathway, originally characterized in Drosophila, is highly conserved in mammals and regulates organ size, cell contact inhibition, proliferation, apoptosis and polarity (Ramos and Camargo, 2012; Yi and Kissil, 2010; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ramos and Camargo, 2012; Yi and Kissil, 2010; Yu et al., 2015.

claim: The Hippo-YAP signaling pathway regulates organ size, cell contact inhibition, proliferation, apoptosis and polarity.
source: The Hippo-YAP signaling pathway, originally characterized in Drosophila, is highly conserved in mammals and regulates organ size, cell contact inhibition, proliferation, apoptosis and polarity (Ramos and Camargo, 2012; Yi and Kissil, 2010; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ramos and Camargo, 2012; Yi and Kissil, 2010; Yu et al., 2015.

claim: MST1/2 promote phosphorylation of WW45 (also known as Sav1), Lats1/2, and MOB1 (MOBKL1A/B).
source: At the core of the mammalian pathway, MST1/2 promote phosphorylation of WW45 (also known as Sav1), Lats1/2, and MOB1 (MOBKL1A/B).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about the Hippo pathway.

claim: Activated Lats1/2 phosphorylates YAP, promoting ubiquitination and proteosomal degradation by a SCFbeta-TRCP E3 ligase.
source: Once activated, Lats1/2 phosphorylates the primary downstream effector YAP, promoting ubiquitination and proteosomal degradation by a SCFbeta-TRCP E3 ligase and sequestering YAP from the nucleus, where it functions as a transcriptional co-activator (Hao et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2010b, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hao et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2010b, 2007.

claim: Lats1/2 phosphorylation of YAP sequesters YAP from the nucleus, where it functions as a transcriptional co-activator.
source: Once activated, Lats1/2 phosphorylates the primary downstream effector YAP, promoting ubiquitination and proteosomal degradation by a SCFbeta-TRCP E3 ligase and sequestering YAP from the nucleus, where it functions as a transcriptional co-activator (Hao et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2010b, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hao et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2010b, 2007.

claim: The DNA-binding TEA domain (TEAD) transcription factors are thought to mediate a YAP-driven pro-proliferative gene expression program.
source: Among the different transcription factors activated by YAP, the DNA-binding TEA domain (TEAD) transcription factors are thought to mediate a YAP-driven pro-proliferative gene expression program (Galli et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2010b, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Galli et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2010b, 2007.

claim: YAP's involvement in cancer has been demonstrated in several tissues, including liver, intestine, heart, pancreas, and brain.
source: YAP's involvement in cancer has been demonstrated in several tissues, including liver, intestine, heart, pancreas, and brain (Yu et al., 2015; Guerrant et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2015 and Guerrant et al., 2016.

claim: YAP plays a key role in developing resistance to RAF- and MEK-targeted therapies in lung and colon cancer cells.
source: Importantly, recent studies revealed YAP plays a key role in developing resistance to RAF- and MEK-targeted therapies in lung and colon cancer cells (Lin et al., 2015) and cancer relapse in KRAS-driven colon and pancreatic cancers (Kapoor et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2015.

claim: YAP plays a key role in cancer relapse in KRAS-driven colon and pancreatic cancers.
source: Importantly, recent studies revealed YAP plays a key role in developing resistance to RAF- and MEK-targeted therapies in lung and colon cancer cells (Lin et al., 2015) and cancer relapse in KRAS-driven colon and pancreatic cancers (Kapoor et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kapoor et al., 2014 and Shao et al., 2014.

claim: Merlin is a tumor suppressor that is inactivated in Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2).
source: Upstream of the core kinase cassette is the tumor suppressor Merlin (moesin-ezrin-radixin-like protein), which is inactivated in Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) (McClatchey et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McClatchey et al., 1998.

claim: Functions for Merlin have been described in the nucleus as well as at the plasma membrane.
source: Functions for Merlin have been described in the nucleus (Li et al., 2014, 2010) as well as at the plasma membrane (Yin et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2014, 2010 for nuclear functions and Yin et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2010 for plasma membrane functions.

claim: In the mouse-liver, homozygous deletion of Nf2 results in tumor formation.
source: In the mouse-liver, homozygous deletion of Nf2 results in tumor formation.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Heterozygous deletion of Yap significantly suppresses the loss-of-Nf2 phenotype, implicating YAP as a major downstream effector of NF2.
source: However, heterozygous deletion of Yap significantly suppresses the loss-of-Nf2 phenotype, thus implicating YAP as a major downstream effector of NF2 (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: Analysis of liver-specific Nf2 knockout mice and Nf2:Amot double knockout (DKO) mice showed Amot is required for hepatic ductal cell proliferation and tumor formation in the context of either Nf2 loss or DDC-induced injury.
source: Analysis of liver-specific Nf2 knockout mice and Nf2:Amot double knockout (DKO) mice showed Amot is required for hepatic ductal cell proliferation and tumor formation in the context of either Nf2 loss or DDC (3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine)-induced injury.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding from the analysis of mouse models.

claim: Substantially increased expression of Amot was observed in NF2-null human schwannomas samples, which primarily displayed localization of Amot in the nucleus.
source: Additionally, substantially increased expression of Amot was observed in NF2-null human schwannomas samples, which primarily displayed localization of Amot in the nucleus (Yi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yi et al., 2013.

claim: In renal cell carcinoma (RCC), Amot promotes the proliferation of renal epithelial and RCC cells.
source: Further evidence demonstrated that in renal cell carcinoma (RCC), Amot promotes the proliferation of renal epithelial and RCC cells, and is crucial for YAP transcriptional activity by promoting its nuclear localization (Lv et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lv et al., 2016.

claim: In renal cell carcinoma, Amot is crucial for YAP transcriptional activity by promoting its nuclear localization.
source: Further evidence demonstrated that in renal cell carcinoma (RCC), Amot promotes the proliferation of renal epithelial and RCC cells, and is crucial for YAP transcriptional activity by promoting its nuclear localization (Lv et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lv et al., 2016.

claim: Amot functions as a negative regulator of YAP activity, as direct association of Amot and YAP results in translocation to cytoplasm/cell junctions.
source: However, it has also been reported that Amot functions as a negative regulator of YAP activity, as direct association of Amot and YAP results in translocation to cytoplasm/cell junctions (Leung and Zernicka-Goetz, 2013; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leung and Zernicka-Goetz, 2013 and Zhao et al., 2011.

claim: Amot acts as a scaffold protein to promote localization of YAP, as well as other Hippo/YAP core kinases, to the cytoplasm/cell junctions/actin cytoskeleton and promote Lats1/2-mediated phosphorylation of YAP.
source: Moreover, a number of studies suggest that Amot acts as a scaffold protein to promote localization of YAP, as well as other Hippo/YAP core kinases, to the cytoplasm/cell junctions/actin cytoskeleton and promote Lats1/2-mediated phosphorylation of YAP (Chan et al., 2011; Dai et al., 2013; Paramasivam et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2011; Dai et al., 2013; Paramasivam et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser175 on human Amot (corresponding to Ser176 in mouse) at the conserved HVRSLS motif by Lats1/2 has been reported as a key post-translational modification controlling Amot function and association with YAP.
source: Phosphorylation of Ser175 on human Amot (corresponding to Ser176 in mouse) at the conserved HVRSLS motif by Lats1/2 has been reported as a key post-translational modification controlling Amot function and association with YAP (Hirate et al., 2013; Moleirinho et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hirate et al., 2013 and Moleirinho et al., 2014.

claim: Amot-p130 functions as a scaffold protein mediating YAP and Merlin association.
source: Here we show that Amot-p130 functions as a scaffold protein mediating YAP and Merlin association and that phosphorylation of Amot at Ser176 induces translocation of the complex from the cytoplasm and nucleus to the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Phosphorylation of Amot at Ser176 induces translocation of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex from the cytoplasm and nucleus to the plasma membrane.
source: Here we show that Amot-p130 functions as a scaffold protein mediating YAP and Merlin association and that phosphorylation of Amot at Ser176 induces translocation of the complex from the cytoplasm and nucleus to the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Relocalization of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex to the plasma membrane significantly impacts the activity of YAP and regulates YAP's ability to promote cell proliferation and tumorigenesis.
source: This relocalization of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex significantly impacts the activity of YAP and regulates YAP's ability to promote cell proliferation and tumorigenesis.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: YAP associates with Merlin in HEK293 cells.
source: First, to determine the interaction between Merlin and YAP, HEK293 cells were transfected with expression vectors for HA-tagged Merlin and V5-tagged YAP. Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) analyses using anti-HA or anti-V5 antibodies revealed association between YAP and Merlin (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The Merlin-YAP interaction was confirmed in hSC2λ immortalized human Schwann cells.
source: The Merlin-YAP interaction was also confirmed in another independent cell type – the hSC2λ immortalized human Schwann cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The association between YAP and Merlin was confirmed at the endogenous protein levels.
source: Importantly, further validation of the association between YAP and Merlin was confirmed at the endogenous protein levels, using antibodies directed against Merlin or YAP (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with endogenous proteins shown in Figure 1C.

claim: YAP associates with Merlin primarily in the nucleus and cytoplasm, and to a much lesser extent at the plasma membrane.
source: These subcellular fractionation studies showed an association between Merlin and YAP primarily in the nucleus and cytoplasm, and to a much lesser extent at the plasma membrane (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Merlin and YAP co-localize predominantly in the cytoplasm and nucleus as shown by immunofluorescence.
source: Further confirmation of Merlin and YAP co-localization was provided by immunofluorescence (IF) staining, in HEK293 and hSC2λ cells, where we observed co-localization of IF signal predominantly in the cytoplasm and nucleus (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In the absence of Amot, YAP and Merlin could no longer be co-immunoprecipitated.
source: Co-IP experiments with HA-tagged Merlin and V5-tagged YAP confirmed that in the absence of Amot, the complex is not formed as YAP and Merlin could no longer be co-immunoprecipitated (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Amot knockdown cells shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Knockdown of Amot using an siRNA smartpool impaired the association of Merlin and YAP.
source: Similarly, knockdown of Amot using an siRNA smartpool impaired the association of Merlin and YAP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Amot-p80 was unable to support the association between Merlin and YAP.
source: As expected, attempting to IP HA-Merlin or V5-YAP demonstrated that Amot-p80 was unable to support the association between these proteins (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with Amot-p80 shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutation of the individual PPEY/LPTY motifs or combinations thereof, significantly impaired the association between Merlin and YAP.
source: Moreover, mutation of the individual PPEY/LPTY motifs or combinations thereof, significantly impaired the association between Merlin and YAP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with Amot mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: All three forms of Amot (wild-type, S176A, and S176E) support the formation of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex.
source: These analyses demonstrated that all three forms of Amot support the formation of the complex, as evidenced by the co-IP of Merlin and YAP (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Amot phosphorylated at S176 binds to both YAP and Merlin.
source: In addition, we examined whether phosphorylated Amot is still able to bind both YAP and Merlin, by using an antibody that specifically binds phosphorylated S176 (p-S176). The antibody was used to IP phosphorylated Amot and co-IP of Merlin and YAP was assessed by western blotting. These experiments showed that Amot phosphorylated at S176 binds to both YAP and Merlin.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments using a phospho-specific antibody.

claim: IP with antibodies against YAP or Merlin showed co-IP with phosphorylated Amot.
source: Similarly, IP with antibodies against YAP or Merlin also showed co-IP with phosphorylated Amot (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Amot S176 phosphorylation state does not affect formation of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex.
source: Collectively, our findings demonstrate that Amot S176 phosphorylation state does not affect formation of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation experiments with different Amot phosphorylation states.

claim: Both phosphorylated YAP and constitutively active YAPS127A mutant retain their ability to associate with Amot/Merlin.
source: Using similar IP approaches described above, we found that both phosphorylated YAP and constitutively active YAPS127A mutant retain their ability to associate with Amot/Merlin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A YAP mutant where five major phosphorylation sites have been abolished (YAP-5A) was no longer associated with the Amot-Merlin complex.
source: Surprisingly, a YAP mutant where five major phosphorylation sites have been abolished (YAP-5A [Zhao et al., 2010b]) was no longer associated with the complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In cells expressing Amot-p130, the majority of this protein localized to cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions, and to a lesser extent in the plasma membrane fraction.
source: In the cells expressing Amot-p130, the majority of this protein localized to cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions, and to a lesser extent in the plasma membrane fraction.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation experiments.

claim: Amot-p130S176A showed a marked increase in nuclear localization and almost no presence at the plasma membrane.
source: Interestingly, Amot-p130S176A showed a marked increase in nuclear localization and almost no presence at the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation experiments.

claim: Amot-p130S176E showed a clear shift in localization towards the cytoplasm and plasma membrane.
source: In contrast, Amot-p130S176E showed a clear shift in localization towards the cytoplasm and plasma membrane (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Fractionation studies from hSC2λ Schwann cells and HepG2 hepatocellular carcinoma cells followed a similar distribution pattern to the transfected 293-shAmot cells.
source: To determine the broader relevance of our findings in HEK293 cells to additional biological systems, we carried out a similar analysis in human hSC2λ Schwann cells and HepG2 hepatocellular carcinoma cells. Fractionation studies from these additional cell types followed a similar distribution pattern to the transfected 293-shAmot cells (Figure 4—figure supplements 1A and 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation experiments in additional cell types shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1A and 2A.

claim: Immunofluorescence analyses confirmed a stronger intensity of Amot in the cytoplasm and nucleus of cells expressing Amot-p130.
source: To complement the biochemical fractionation studies, we assessed localization of the different Amot proteins by IF staining in the 293-shAmot cells. These analyses confirmed the fractionation findings, demonstrating a stronger intensity of Amot in the cytoplasm and nucleus of cells expressing Amot-p130, a shift to nuclear staining in Amot-p130S176A expressing cells and cytoplasmic/plasma membrane localization in Amot-p130S176E expressing cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Immunofluorescence showed a shift to nuclear staining in Amot-p130S176A expressing cells.
source: To complement the biochemical fractionation studies, we assessed localization of the different Amot proteins by IF staining in the 293-shAmot cells. These analyses confirmed the fractionation findings, demonstrating a stronger intensity of Amot in the cytoplasm and nucleus of cells expressing Amot-p130, a shift to nuclear staining in Amot-p130S176A expressing cells and cytoplasmic/plasma membrane localization in Amot-p130S176E expressing cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Immunofluorescence showed cytoplasmic/plasma membrane localization in Amot-p130S176E expressing cells.
source: To complement the biochemical fractionation studies, we assessed localization of the different Amot proteins by IF staining in the 293-shAmot cells. These analyses confirmed the fractionation findings, demonstrating a stronger intensity of Amot in the cytoplasm and nucleus of cells expressing Amot-p130, a shift to nuclear staining in Amot-p130S176A expressing cells and cytoplasmic/plasma membrane localization in Amot-p130S176E expressing cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In 293-shAmot cells transfected with Amot-p130 and YAP, Amot co-IPed with YAP mainly in the cytoplasm but also in the nucleus with little to no interaction detected at the plasma membrane.
source: In agreement with our previous results, in 293-shAmot cells transfected with Amot-p130 and YAP, Amot co-IPed with YAP mainly in the cytoplasm but also in the nucleus with little to no interaction detected at the plasma membrane (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in subcellular fractions shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In cells expressing the Amot-p130S176A allele, the Amot-YAP complex mainly localized to the nucleus with little to no interaction detected in the cytoplasm and plasma membrane.
source: Importantly, in cells expressing the Amot-p130S176A allele, the Amot-YAP complex mainly localized to the nucleus with little to no interaction detected in the cytoplasm and plasma membrane (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in subcellular fractions shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In cells expressing the Amot-p130S176E allele an increase in the Amot-YAP association was detected at the plasma membrane, in addition to the cytoplasmic fraction, with little to no interaction detected in the nucleus.
source: Significantly, in cells expressing the Amot-p130S176E allele an increase in the Amot-YAP association was detected at the plasma membrane, in addition to the cytoplasmic fraction. Little to no interaction was detected in the nucleus (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in subcellular fractions shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The distribution of Amot/YAP complex mimics the distribution observed for Amot.
source: Thus, the distribution of Amot/YAP complex mimics the distribution observed for Amot (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from comparing the distribution patterns of Amot and the Amot/YAP complex.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis showed the localization of YAP and Merlin to the plasma membrane is significantly enhanced in cells expressing the Amot-p130S176E allele.
source: These findings were extended and confirmed by IF analysis of the YAP-Merlin association in 293-shAmot cells, where the localization of YAP and Merlin to the plasma membrane is significantly enhanced in cells expressing the Amot-p130S176E allele (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: AmotS176 phosphorylation does not impact the formation of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex, but mediates the localization of the complex.
source: Overall our findings demonstrate that while AmotS176 phosphorylation does not impact the formation of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex, it mediates the localization of the complex through phosphorylation of Serine 176 that leads to recruitment of the complex to the plasma membrane or a shift to a nuclear localization in the hypophosphorylated state.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation and localization experiments.

claim: Phosphorylation of Serine 176 leads to recruitment of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex to the plasma membrane.
source: Overall our findings demonstrate that while AmotS176 phosphorylation does not impact the formation of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex, it mediates the localization of the complex through phosphorylation of Serine 176 that leads to recruitment of the complex to the plasma membrane or a shift to a nuclear localization in the hypophosphorylated state.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation and localization experiments.

claim: Hypophosphorylation of Amot at Serine 176 leads to a shift to nuclear localization of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex.
source: Overall our findings demonstrate that while AmotS176 phosphorylation does not impact the formation of the Amot/YAP/Merlin complex, it mediates the localization of the complex through phosphorylation of Serine 176 that leads to recruitment of the complex to the plasma membrane or a shift to a nuclear localization in the hypophosphorylated state.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation and localization experiments.

claim: Flag-tagged Patj strongly associates with Amot-p130S176E, compared to weaker or null interaction with Amot-p130 and Amot-p130S176A, respectively.
source: Using co-IP, we found that Flag-tagged Patj strongly associates with Amot-p130S176E, compared to weaker or null interaction with Amot-p130 and Amot-p130S176A, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: IP of the different Amot forms demonstrated a stronger association between Patj and Amot-p130S176E.
source: In a reciprocal approach, IP of the different Amot forms demonstrated a stronger association between Patj and Amot-p130S176E (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Pals1 was consistently able to co-IP with Amot-p130S176E, but this association was greatly diminished with Amot-p130S176A or wild type Amot-p130.
source: Similar results were obtained when examining the association of Pals1 or E-cadherin with Amot. While we were consistently able to co-IP Pals1 or E-cadherin with Amot-p130S176E, this association was greatly diminished with Amot-p130S176A or wild type Amot-p130 (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: E-cadherin was consistently able to co-IP with Amot-p130S176E, but this association was greatly diminished with Amot-p130S176A or wild type Amot-p130.
source: Similar results were obtained when examining the association of Pals1 or E-cadherin with Amot. While we were consistently able to co-IP Pals1 or E-cadherin with Amot-p130S176E, this association was greatly diminished with Amot-p130S176A or wild type Amot-p130 (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Localization of phosphorylated Amot-p130 to the cell membrane is mediated through interactions with components of junctional structures.
source: These findings suggest that localization of phosphorylated Amot-p130 to the cell membrane is mediated through interactions with components of junctional structures, which remain to be identified.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing association with junctional proteins.

claim: Similar amounts of all Amot proteins (wild-type, S176A, and S176E) were present in F-actin pull downs.
source: As shown in Figure 5F, similar amounts of all Amot proteins were present in the pull downs (Upper panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by F-actin pull-down experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Similar levels of Actin were present in all pull downs indicating the expression of the different Amot alleles did not affect cellular levels of F-actin.
source: Importantly, similar levels of Actin were present in all pull downs indicating the expression of the different Amot alleles did not affect cellular levels of F-actin (Lower panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by F-actin pull-down experiments shown in Figure 5F.
